g9-economics-ue8-t1.overview: Entrepreneurship turns ideas into businesses, and the entrepreneur is the person who takes the risk to do it. This lesson defines enterprise, entrepreneur and entrepreneurship, traces their history, and introduces social entrepreneurship with Ethiopian examples.
objectives: Define the concepts of enterprise, entrepreneur and entrepreneurship
Distinguish the three concepts from one another
Outline the five critical elements of the entrepreneurial process
Trace the historical development of the word entrepreneur
Explain social entrepreneurship and its role in society
g9-economics-ue8-t1.simple: An enterprise is a legal entity that owns the right to conduct business on its own: it can sign contracts, own property, take on liabilities and open bank accounts. An entrepreneur is any person who creates and develops a business idea and takes the risk of setting up an enterprise to produce a product or service that satisfies customer needs. Entrepreneurship is the process of identifying opportunities in the marketplace, arranging the resources required, and investing them for long-term gains. Entrepreneurship shifts people from being job seekers to job creators, which is critical in countries like Ethiopia with high unemployment. Famous Ethiopian entrepreneurs include Bethlehem Tilahun Alemu, founder of SoleRebels, and Haile Gebrselassie, owner of Marathon Motors.
g9-economics-ue8-t1.detailed:
Enterprise. An enterprise is defined as a legal entity possessing the right to conduct business on its own. For example, it can enter into contracts, own property, incur liabilities and establish bank accounts. The enterprise is therefore the organisation - the business itself - while a person stands behind it.

Entrepreneur. An entrepreneur is any person who creates and develops a business idea and takes the risk of setting up an enterprise to produce a product or service which satisfies customer needs. The word comes from the French concept entrepreneur, which matches closely with the English concept of business conduct. An entrepreneur is commonly seen as an innovator, a source of new ideas, goods, services and business procedures.

Entrepreneurship. Entrepreneurship is the process of identifying opportunities in the marketplace, arranging the resources required to pursue these opportunities, and investing resources in order to exploit the opportunities for long term gains. It involves creating incremental wealth by bringing together resources in new ways to start and operate an enterprise. Entrepreneurship is a practice and a process that results in creativity, innovation and enterprise development and growth.

Why entrepreneurship matters in Ethiopia. Engaging in entrepreneurship shifts people from being job seekers to job creators. This is critical in a country that has a high rate of unemployment like Ethiopia, because more job creators mean more employment for others. However, entrepreneurship requires a lot of creativity as the driving force behind innovation.

Ethiopian entrepreneurs. Bethlehem Tilahun Alemu started a business at 25, immediately after graduating from college. She founded SoleRebels, a shoe company that uses recycled tires, and in 2014 Forbes named it the fastest growing brand in Africa. Haile Gebrselassie, the retired long-distance runner and national hero, is also a successful businessman considered one of the richest people in Ethiopia. He owns Marathon Motors, which assembles Hyundai vehicles and rolled out its first electric car from the assembly plant. Haile invests in hospitality, entertainment, real estate, agriculture and technology and employs over 3000 people across his businesses.

Five critical elements of the process. The process of entrepreneurship includes: (1) the ability to spot a potentially profitable opportunity; (2) the ability to commercialise the perceived opportunity, also called innovation; (3) the ability to pursue it in the long term; (4) the ability to pursue it methodically; and (5) acceptance of failure as a possibility.

History and social entrepreneurship. In the ancient period an entrepreneur was a person managing large commercial projects with resources provided to him. In the 17th century, a person who signed a contractual agreement with the government to provide stipulated products or services was an entrepreneur, with a fixed price so profit or loss reflected his effort. In the 18th century Richard Cantillon developed the first theory, saying an entrepreneur is a risk-taker, and the entrepreneurial role was differentiated from the capital-providing role. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries the entrepreneur was viewed economically as one who organises and operates an enterprise for personal gain, and in the mid-twentieth century as an inventor. Social entrepreneurship is the process by which individuals, start-ups and entrepreneurs develop and find solutions that directly address social issues; a social entrepreneur explores business opportunities with a positive impact on the community, society or the world, like Muhammad Yunus and Steve Jobs.

keyTerms.def: A legal entity possessing the right to conduct business on its own, for example entering contracts, owning property, incurring liabilities and establishing bank accounts.
Any person who creates and develops a business idea and takes the risk of setting up an enterprise to produce a product or service that satisfies customer needs.
The process of identifying opportunities in the marketplace, arranging resources to pursue them, and investing for long-term gains; creating incremental wealth by combining resources in new ways.
A person who starts a business and employs others, instead of looking for employment as a job seeker does.
Cantillon's description of the entrepreneur: a person who operates at risk, since buying at a known price and selling at an unknown price can bring profit or loss.
The process by which individuals, start-ups and entrepreneurs develop and find solutions that directly address social issues, driving social change with benefit to society.
A person who explores business opportunities that have a positive impact on their community, society or the world.

workedExamples.problem: A graduate has the idea of turning old tires into shoe soles. Identify the enterprise, the entrepreneur and the entrepreneurship in this story.
workedExamples.given: A business idea exists, and a person must decide whether to take the risk of starting it.
workedExamples.formula: Concept test: enterprise = the organization; entrepreneur = the risk-taking person; entrepreneurship = the process of pursuing opportunity.
workedExamples.substitution: The registered shoe company is the enterprise; the graduate who takes the risk is the entrepreneur; the whole act of spotting the opportunity, arranging resources and investing is entrepreneurship.
workedExamples.calculation: Each concept matches a different part of the same story, so the three terms are related but not the same.
workedExamples.answer: The company is the enterprise, the graduate is the entrepreneur, and the opportunity-pursuing process is entrepreneurship.

workedExamples.problem: Ethiopia has a high rate of unemployment. Explain how entrepreneurship helps solve this economic problem.
workedExamples.given: Many people seek jobs; few businesses exist to employ them.
workedExamples.formula: Reasoning: entrepreneurship shifts people from job seekers to job creators.
workedExamples.substitution: When an entrepreneur starts an enterprise such as a shoe factory, workers are hired.
workedExamples.calculation: Each new enterprise creates employment directly and adds products and income to the economy.
workedExamples.answer: Entrepreneurship creates job creators whose enterprises employ the unemployed and raise national output.

workedExamples.problem: A merchant buys a shipment at a known price and will sell it at an unknown price in a distant market. Using Cantillon's theory, is this person acting as an entrepreneur?
workedExamples.given: Selling price is unknown in advance, so profit or loss is uncertain.
workedExamples.formula: Cantillon: an entrepreneur is a risk-taker who operates under uncertainty.
workedExamples.substitution: Buying at a known price and selling at an unknown price is exactly operating at risk.
workedExamples.calculation: The decision faces uncertain returns, so the merchant shows entrepreneurial risk-taking.
workedExamples.answer: Yes, under Cantillon's 18th century theory this merchant is acting at risk like an entrepreneur.

workedExamples.problem: Haile Gebrselassie employs over 3000 people across hospitality, entertainment, real estate, agriculture and technology. What does this show about the role of entrepreneurs in economic development?
workedExamples.given: One entrepreneur owns businesses in many sectors and employs thousands.
workedExamples.formula: Role test: entrepreneurs organise resources and create employment.
workedExamples.substitution: Across five sectors, one entrepreneur provides income for over 3000 people.
workedExamples.calculation: Employment, output and taxes all rise, so entrepreneurs are engines of development.
workedExamples.answer: Entrepreneurs create jobs, expand output across sectors and drive economic development.

commonMistakes: Using enterprise, entrepreneur and entrepreneurship as if they were the same word.
Thinking an enterprise must be a large company; even a small sole proprietorship is an enterprise.
Believing all business persons are entrepreneurs, when entrepreneurship requires creating a business idea and taking risk.
Forgetting that accepting possible failure is one of the five critical elements of entrepreneurship.
Assuming entrepreneurs are only interested in profit, ignoring social entrepreneurs who target social change.
Thinking only famous people like Haile Gebrselassie can be entrepreneurs; any person with an idea and the willingness to take risk can be one.
applications: spotting an unmet need in your kebele, such as affordable shoemaking, and planning an enterprise to serve it.
Registering a small enterprise with government offices so it can have bank accounts and sign contracts.
Following the example of SoleRebels by building a business around recycled local materials.
Choosing to create a job for yourself and others after school instead of waiting for employment.
Learning the story of Ethiopian entrepreneurs like Bethlehem Tilahun Alemu as models for your own plans.
g9-economics-ue8-t1.summary: An enterprise is the legal business entity, the entrepreneur is the person who takes the risk to create it, and entrepreneurship is the process of turning market opportunities into long-term gains. The concept has evolved from Cantillon's risk-taker to the modern innovator. Entrepreneurship turns job seekers into job creators, which is vital for economies like Ethiopia's.

g9-economics-ue8-t2.overview: Creativity generates new ideas and innovation applies them, and together they drive entrepreneurship and national economic growth. This lesson defines creativity and innovation, lists the four types of innovation, and shows how the three concepts connect.
objectives: Define creativity and identify its three key elements
Define innovation and explain its place in the entrepreneurial process
List the four distinct types of innovation with examples
Explain the relationship among creativity, innovation and entrepreneurship
Show how creativity and innovation can solve local problems profitably
g9-economics-ue8-t2.simple: Creativity is the tendency to generate ideas, alternatives or possibilities that may be useful in solving problems and communicating with others. It is an ongoing process that produces ideas with potential value by recombining things we already know in unexpected ways. Innovation lies at the heart of the entrepreneurial process; it is the implementation of a new idea. The four types of innovation are invention (creating a new product, service or process), expansion (growing one), duplication (replicating one) and synthesis (combining existing concepts into a new formulation). Creativity generates new ways of doing business, innovation applies them, and together they give the entrepreneur efficiency and a competitive advantage.
g9-economics-ue8-t2.detailed:
Creativity defined. Creativity is the tendency to generate ideas, alternatives or possibilities that may be useful in solving problems, communicating with others, and entertaining ourselves and others. It is the ability to come up with new ideas and to identify new and different ways of looking at problems and opportunities. It is a process of assembling ideas by recombining elements already known but wrongly assumed to be unrelated to each other. To be creative you must be able to view things in new ways from different perspectives.

Three key elements of creativity. First, creativity is an ongoing process that never stops. Second, it results in ideas that have potential value. Third, it works by recombining: putting things together in unexpected ways. Creativity is the development of original and potentially useful ideas about products, practises, services or procedures for an organisation.

Innovation defined. Innovation lies at the heart of the entrepreneurial process and is a means to the exploitation of opportunities. It is the implementation of a new idea at an individual, group or organisational level. An innovation is a process by which a domain, product or service is renewed and brought up to date by applying new processes, introducing new techniques, or establishing successful ideas to create new value.

Four types of innovation. An invention is the creation of a new product, service or process. Expansion is the growth or extension of a product, service or process. Duplication is the replication of an already existing product, service or process. Synthesis is the combination of existing concepts and factors into a new formulation. Recognising which type you are planning helps you judge the risk, cost and competition you will face.

From creativity to entrepreneurship. Creativity, innovation and entrepreneurship are chronologically interrelated and are recognised as important contributors to a nation's economic growth. Creativity produces the novel idea; innovation applies that creative solution to improve people's lives or enrich society; entrepreneurship then organises the resources to deliver it to the market. Exploring new niches and coming up with new ideas leads to efficiency, which eventually gives an entrepreneur a competitive advantage.

Solving local problems. For an Ethiopian student, creativity starts with looking at nearby problems: waste that could be recycled, long queues for a common service, farmers needing cheap tools. A creative solution - such as turning recycled tires into shoes, as SoleRebels did - becomes an innovation once it is implemented, and becomes entrepreneurship once resources are organised to serve customers. Creative entrepreneurs are investors in talent, their own or other people's; the most renowned have combined creative flair with entrepreneurial ability to build multimillion-dollar business empires, including Haile Gebrselassie.

keyTerms.def: The tendency to generate ideas, alternatives or possibilities useful in solving problems; assembling ideas by recombining elements already known but wrongly assumed to be unrelated.
The implementation of a new idea at an individual, group or organisational level; a means to the exploitation of opportunities.
The creation of a new product, service or process.
The growth of a product, service or process.
The replication of an already existing product, service or process.
The combination of existing concepts and factors into a new formulation.
The edge a firm gains, for example through efficiency from new ideas, when it serves customers better than its rivals.
An entrepreneur who combines creative flair with business ability; an investor in talent, their own or other people's.

workedExamples.problem: A student notices that plastic bottles litter the market in her town. Show how she could move from creativity to innovation to entrepreneurship.
workedExamples.given: A problem exists locally; no business currently uses the waste.
workedExamples.formula: Chain: creativity generates the idea; innovation implements it; entrepreneurship organises resources for the market.
workedExamples.substitution: Idea: collect bottles and make flower pots or building materials. Implementation: set up a workshop and produce. Organisation: hire workers, buy tools, sell to customers.
workedExamples.calculation: Each stage adds value: waste is cleaned at low cost and sold as useful products, earning profit while solving the litter problem.
workedExamples.answer: Creative idea, implemented as a new product, organised into a small enterprise that turns waste into income.

workedExamples.problem: A firm copies the design of an existing mobile money service and offers it in an underserved region. Which type of innovation is this?
workedExamples.given: The product already exists elsewhere; nothing new is invented.
workedExamples.formula: Type test: invention creates new, duplication replicates existing, synthesis combines, expansion grows.
workedExamples.substitution: The firm replicates an already existing service rather than creating a new one.
workedExamples.calculation: Moving an existing service to a new place matches the definition of duplication.
workedExamples.answer: Duplication.

workedExamples.problem: An entrepreneur combines an old generator, a bicycle frame and a grinding mill into one cheap machine for village flour milling. Classify this creativity.
workedExamples.given: The parts are known, but nothing combined them before.
workedExamples.formula: Definition: creativity is recombining elements already known but wrongly assumed to be unrelated.
workedExamples.substitution: Three existing items are put together in an unexpected way.
workedExamples.calculation: The recombination of known elements is exactly what the creativity definition describes.
workedExamples.answer: This is creativity through recombination, and the product is a synthesis-type innovation.

workedExamples.problem: Explain why creativity alone does not make a successful entrepreneur.
workedExamples.given: A person has many ideas but implements none.
workedExamples.formula: Cause-effect: ideas have value only when implemented and commercialised.
workedExamples.substitution: Without innovation, an idea stays in the head; without organising resources, no customer is served.
workedExamples.calculation: The chain must be completed: idea, implementation, market delivery.
workedExamples.answer: Because entrepreneurship needs innovation to implement ideas and resources to reach the market, not just ideas.

commonMistakes: Thinking creativity and innovation are the same; creativity makes ideas, innovation implements them.
Believing only inventions count as innovation, ignoring expansion, duplication and synthesis.
Assuming creative people are born, not made; creativity can be practised by viewing problems from different perspectives.
Confusing duplication with invention.
applications: Recycling local waste such as tires or bottles into products, following the SoleRebels model.
Setting up brainstorming clubs at school to generate ideas that solve campus problems.
Improving an existing service in your village, such as faster grain milling, through synthesis of existing tools.
Using creativity before innovation in designing products, since exploring new niches leads to efficiency and competitive advantage.
Contributing ideas that raise national economic growth, since creativity, innovation and entrepreneurship feed it.
g9-economics-ue8-t2.summary: Creativity is the ongoing generation of valuable new ideas by recombining known elements in unexpected ways; innovation implements those ideas, and its four types are invention, expansion, duplication and synthesis. The three concepts of creativity, innovation and entrepreneurship are chronologically interrelated and together drive national economic growth.

g9-economics-ue8-t3.overview: A successful entrepreneur is made less by money than by a way of thinking. This lesson describes the entrepreneurial mind-set, the five key attitudes every entrepreneur must have, and the general and people management skills that turn ideas into reality.
objectives: Define the entrepreneurial mind-set and explain its importance
Describe the five key attitudes: passion, bravery, flexibility, strong work ethics and integrity
Explain how entrepreneurs should treat failure
Classify management skills into general and people management skills
Assess your own skills and attributes to become more innovative
g9-economics-ue8-t3.simple: An entrepreneurial mind-set is a state of mind that enables a person to undertake entrepreneurial activities. Entrepreneurs are brave in their decisions, actively seek clients and take risks; a successful entrepreneur fails at least once, and what matters is learning from failure. The five key attitudes are passion, bravery, flexibility, strong work ethics and integrity. A skill is knowledge demonstrated through action, and turning an idea into reality needs two kinds: general management skills (strategy, planning, marketing, financial, project management, time management) and people management skills (communication, leadership, motivation, delegation, negotiation). Entrepreneurial performance comes from combining business knowledge, these skills and personal motivation.
g9-economics-ue8-t3.detailed:
The entrepreneurial mind-set. An entrepreneurial mind-set is a state of mind that an individual possesses. The way people think and their attitude towards the pursuit of their goals is an important tool that enables them to undertake entrepreneurial activities. Entrepreneurs are innovators and creators who, because of their way of thinking, give their business the best chance of surviving: they are brave in the decisions they make, they actively seek clients and they take risks. Not all entrepreneurs succeed in every business activity. A successful entrepreneur fails at least once; what matters is how they learn from their failures and exploit them.

Passion. Entrepreneurs should be passionate about their ideas, goals and companies. This passion is what drives them to do their business. Whatever drives an individual to try to succeed is where his or her passion lies, and that passion is essential to entrepreneurial life.

Bravery. Entrepreneurs fear that they will not succeed, in the sense that a well-conceived idea cannot be executed. However, they do not let these fears of failure inhibit them. Being brave, they learn from their failures and use their fear of failing to push them to work hard and correct the mistakes that caused them to fail. Thus bravery drives them to pursue successful businesses.

Flexibility. Entrepreneurs usually experience obstacles and difficulties. They must possess flexible mind-sets so they can change in a way that seems to lead towards failure. Flexible entrepreneurs modify the route towards their established goal in order to achieve it successfully.

Strong work ethics and integrity. Starting from the ground up is not easy: many hours of hard work, frustration, creativity and supervision go into a new business, and entrepreneurs are always working, establishing new ideas, creating new products, designing new processes and hiring clever people. Entrepreneurs must also demonstrate that they are trustworthy and honest. Suppliers need to know that payments will arrive on time; customers need to know that orders will be delivered as promised; colleagues need to know they are valued; investors need to know the company has potential to grow.

Skills to be more innovative. A skill is knowledge demonstrated through action - the ability to perform in a certain way. Turning an idea into reality depends on two kinds of skills. General management skills organise the company's physical and financial resources: strategy skills (seeing the business as a whole and how it beats competitors), planning skills (considering what the future may hold), marketing skills (seeing how offerings satisfy customer needs), financial skills (managing money, expenses, cash flow and investment risks), project management skills (objectives, timelines and resources in the right place) and time management skills (prioritising tasks). People management skills guide people inside and outside the firm: communication skills (expressing ideas orally and in writing), leadership skills (inspiring people), motivational skills, delegation skills (allocating tasks) and negotiation skills (maximising outcomes for all parties). Entrepreneurial performance results from a combination of business knowledge, general management skills, people skills and personal motivation.

keyTerms.def: A state of mind that enables an individual to undertake entrepreneurial activities and bravely pursue goals.
The strong drive towards one's ideas, goals and company that motivates entrepreneurial effort.
The courage to act despite fear of failure, and to use failures as lessons to work harder.
The willingness to modify the route towards an established goal when obstacles arise.
The readiness to work many hours with diligence, creativity and supervision to build a business.
Being trustworthy and honest with suppliers, customers, colleagues and investors.
Knowledge that is demonstrated through action; the ability to perform in a certain way.
The ability to allocate tasks to different people, based on their skills and business needs.

workedExamples.problem: A young shop owner's first bakery fails after six months. She plans a second attempt after studying why hers collapsed. Which entrepreneurial attitude is she showing, and why does it matter?
workedExamples.given: She has failed once and is trying again with lessons learned.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: a successful entrepreneur fails at least once and learns from failures.
workedExamples.substitution: She analysed her mistakes and corrects them in the second attempt.
workedExamples.calculation: Learning from failure converts a loss into experience, raising the chance of the next success.
workedExamples.answer: Bravery combined with a learning mind-set; failure becomes a source of improvement.

workedExamples.problem: A supplier is asked to ship goods on credit to a new enterprise. Which attitude of the entrepreneur will most influence the supplier's decision?
workedExamples.given: The supplier wants assurance that payment will arrive on time.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: integrity means suppliers trust that payments will arrive on time.
workedExamples.substitution: The entrepreneur has always paid previous suppliers exactly as promised.
workedExamples.calculation: Trust reduces perceived risk, so the supplier agrees to supply.
workedExamples.answer: Integrity: being trustworthy and honest builds the trust that keeps suppliers willing.

workedExamples.problem: An entrepreneur notices that customers no longer want his original product but want a related service more. Classify the needed attitude and the right response.
workedExamples.given: Market demand has shifted away from the original goal.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: flexible entrepreneurs modify the route towards their established goal.
workedExamples.substitution: He can keep the same goal, serving customers successfully, but change the product route.
workedExamples.calculation: Changing the route rather than abandoning the goal fits the definition of flexibility.
workedExamples.answer: Flexibility: adjust the route to the goal instead of sticking rigidly to the original product.

workedExamples.problem: List which skill category covers: keeping track of expenses, and inspiring workers to complete tasks.
workedExamples.given: One task concerns money management, the other guiding people.
workedExamples.formula: Classification: general management skills organise resources; people management skills guide people.
workedExamples.substitution: Expense tracking is financial skills; inspiring workers is leadership skills.
workedExamples.calculation: Financial skills fall under general management; leadership falls under people management.
workedExamples.answer: Financial skills are general management; leadership skills are people management.

commonMistakes: Thinking entrepreneurs never fear failure; they fear it but do not let the fear inhibit them.
Believing failure means the person is not entrepreneurial, when successful entrepreneurs fail at least once and learn from it.
Confusing flexibility with abandoning goals; flexibility changes the route, not the goal.
Assuming passion alone is enough without long hours of hard work and supervision.
Treating integrity as optional with customers or suppliers, when trust is essential to every party.
Listing only people management skills and forgetting general management skills such as planning and financial skills.
Believing skills are fixed at birth instead of abilities to be improved by identifying strengths and weaknesses.
applications: Writing down which of the five attitudes you possess and which you need to develop before starting a business.
Keeping honest records and paying suppliers on time to build a reputation for integrity.
Practising communication skills by presenting your business idea clearly to classmates or a micro-finance officer.
Delegating chores in a group project according to each member's skills, as an effective entrepreneur does.
Using fear of failure as motivation to prepare harder before a school business bazaar.
g9-economics-ue8-t3.summary: The entrepreneurial mind-set enables brave decisions, active search for clients and calculated risk-taking. The five key attitudes are passion, bravery, flexibility, strong work ethics and integrity, and failure is treated as a lesson rather than an ending. Success also requires general management skills and people management skills, combined with business knowledge and personal motivation.

g9-economics-ue8-t4.overview: Not every idea is worth pursuing; only some become opportunities. This lesson explains how ideas become entrepreneurial opportunities, introduces Schumpeter's creative destruction, and lists the five windows for finding new business opportunities.
objectives: Define an entrepreneurial opportunity and distinguish it from an idea
Describe how opportunities are found: deliberate search, chance and problem solving
Explain Schumpeter's concept of creative destruction
List Schumpeter's five methods for finding new business opportunities
Classify opportunities as demand, supply or technological innovations
g9-economics-ue8-t4.simple: Aspiring entrepreneurs generate ideas all day, but not every idea is worth pursuing. An entrepreneurial opportunity is the point at which identifiable consumer demand meets the possibility of satisfying the requested product or service. Opportunities may be found through deliberate search, may emerge by chance, but most often arise from recognising a problem and trying to solve it. In the 20th century, economist Joseph Schumpeter argued that entrepreneurial innovation is a disruptive force that creates and sustains economic growth while destroying established companies and making products out-dated; he called this creative destruction. He identified five windows of opportunity, from developing a new market for an existing product to using new technology for a new product.
g9-economics-ue8-t4.detailed:
From idea to opportunity. Aspiring entrepreneurs can come up with ideas all day long, but not every idea is necessarily a good one. For an idea to be worth pursuing, we must determine whether it can be converted into an entrepreneurial opportunity. An entrepreneurial opportunity is the point at which identifiable consumer demand meets the possibility of satisfying the requested product or service. Specific criteria must be met to move from an idea into an opportunity. It begins with developing the right mind-set: sharpening your senses on consumer needs and conducting research to determine whether the idea can become a successful new project.

How opportunities are found. In some cases opportunities are found through a deliberate search, especially when developing new technologies. In other instances opportunities emerge unintentionally by chance. In most cases, however, an entrepreneurial opportunity arises from recognising a problem and making a concerted effort to solve it. This is why alertness to the problems around you is itself an economic skill.

Creative destruction. In the 20th century, economist Joseph Schumpeter stated that entrepreneurial innovation is the disruptive force that creates and sustains economic growth. But in the process it can also destroy established companies, reshape businesses and interrupt employment. He termed this force creative destruction. Schumpeter described business processes such as reduction, designed to increase company efficiency. Change in business development improves our lifestyle, but it can make other activities or products out-dated - for example, when a new technology makes an old product unnecessary.

Schumpeter's five windows. Schumpeter identified these methods for finding new business opportunities: (1) develop a new market for an existing product; (2) find at least one new source of resources that would allow the entrepreneur to manufacture the product at a low cost; (3) use existing technology to produce an old product in a new way; (4) use an existing technology to produce a new product; and (5) use new technology to produce a new product.

Classifying the windows. We can understand theories of opportunity as related to supply or demand, or as approaches to innovation in the use of technology. The first situation is a demand opportunity, whereas the second is a supply situation. The last three are technological innovations. For an Ethiopian student, the windows suggest where to look: open existing products to a new region or market, find cheaper local resource sources, apply known technology in new ways, and watch for new technologies that enable entirely new products.

A thought for a product or service that is not yet tested against real consumer demand.
Actively looking for opportunities, especially when developing new technologies.
Schumpeter's term for innovation that creates and sustains economic growth while destroying established companies and making old products out-dated.
An opportunity that comes from developing a new market for an existing product.
An opportunity based on a new source of resources that allows production at low cost.
Using existing or new technology to produce old products in new ways or new products.
The entrepreneur's sensitivity to consumer needs and to problems that hide business opportunities.

workedExamples.problem: A student has an idea to sell tea in a small town. How can she test whether it is an entrepreneurial opportunity?
workedExamples.given: An idea exists; its market value is unknown.
workedExamples.formula: Test: does identifiable consumer demand meet the possibility of satisfying it?
workedExamples.substitution: She researches how many people want tea, what they pay now, and whether she can supply it profitably.
workedExamples.calculation: If real consumer demand exists and she can satisfy it, the idea passes the test.
workedExamples.answer: Only if she confirms identifiable consumer demand can her idea be converted into an entrepreneurial opportunity.

workedExamples.problem: A farmer who sells teff only in his own village begins transporting and selling it in a distant city where it is scarce. Which of Schumpeter's windows does this use?
workedExamples.given: The product is existing; the market is new to it.
workedExamples.formula: Window 1: develop a new market for an existing product.
workedExamples.substitution: The teff is old, but the city buyers are a new market.
workedExamples.calculation: Matching an existing product to a new market is exactly the first window.
workedExamples.answer: The first window: a new market for an existing product, a demand opportunity.

workedExamples.problem: A workshop finds a cheaper local supplier of scrap metal, cutting its cost. Which window is used, and what type is it?
workedExamples.given: A new source of resources lowers production cost.
workedExamples.formula: Window 2: a new source of resources allows manufacture at low cost.
workedExamples.substitution: Cheaper scrap metal is the new resource source.
workedExamples.calculation: Low-cost inputs raise profit margins without changing the product.
workedExamples.answer: The second window; it is a supply situation.

workedExamples.problem: Explain how the spread of mobile phones in Ethiopia illustrates creative destruction.
workedExamples.given: New technology spreads widely and displaces older ways.
workedExamples.formula: Creative destruction: innovation creates growth while destroying established businesses.
workedExamples.substitution: Mobile phones created new services and growth, while reducing demand for older communication services.
workedExamples.calculation: Gains for consumers and new firms came together with losses for displaced firms.
workedExamples.answer: The new technology grew the economy and improved life, but made some established services out-dated.

commonMistakes: Treating every idea as an opportunity without testing for identifiable consumer demand.
Forgetting that most opportunities come from solving problems, not from luck.
Thinking creative destruction is only beneficial; it also destroys established companies and interrupts employment.
Counting all five Schumpeter methods as demand opportunities when only the first is demand-based and the second is supply.
Looking for opportunities only abroad, ignoring problems in your own surroundings.
Assuming new technology wipes out opportunity, when each new window also creates new products and markets.
applications: Listing the entrepreneurial opportunities in your own surroundings, such as unmet needs in transport, food or repairs.
Finding a new market for an existing local product, like selling village honey in a city supermarket.
Searching for cheaper local resource sources so your school enterprise can manufacture at low cost.
Applying an existing technology, like mobile banking, in a new way for rural customers.
Studying how Schumpeter's creative destruction explains why some Ethiopian factories close while new ones open.
g9-economics-ue8-t4.summary: An entrepreneurial opportunity exists where identifiable consumer demand meets the possibility of supplying it; ideas must be tested and researched before they qualify. Most opportunities come from recognising and solving problems. Schumpeter's creative destruction shows that innovation drives growth while displacing old firms, and his five windows range from new markets for old products to new technology for new products.

g9-economics-ue8-t5.overview: Even the most talented leader needs a strong team. This lesson explains five reasons why teamwork matters for business success and shows how diversity in a team raises creativity and performance.
objectives: Explain why even successful leaders need strong teams
Describe how teamwork fosters cooperation and broadens perspectives
Explain how teamwork raises productivity and creates learning opportunities
Show how teamwork shapes a company's culture
Assess the benefit of diversity in entrepreneurial teams
g9-economics-ue8-t5.simple: Although many companies praise a few top employees, recent productivity studies show that even successful leaders need a strong team to succeed. Teamwork matters in five ways: it fosters cooperation, like football players passing to a teammate with a better chance; it broadens perspectives beyond one person's single view; it increases productivity by sharing the workload among people with different skills; it provides opportunities for members to learn from one another; and it shapes a positive company culture of friendship, loyalty and trust. Studies show diverse teams are more creative and perform better by up to 35 percent compared to non-diverse teams.
g9-economics-ue8-t5.detailed:
Why teamwork matters. Many companies emphasise ability and the idea that a few top employees are responsible for most of the success. However, recent productivity studies have shown that even successful leaders need the help of a strong team in order to succeed. As a result, companies are spending millions on team-building strategies, because most recent studies confirm that the value of teamwork is decisive.

1. Teamwork fosters cooperation. Cooperation among teammates is one of the key elements of success. Football teams in which players pass the ball to teammates with better chances of scoring win championships more often than teams whose star players keep 'hero status' and take the shot alone even when others had better chances. The same is true for every team with a common goal: sharing experience and ideas brings better results for all parties and for the whole company.

2. Collaboration broadens perspectives. Working alone gives you only a single perspective, which can be very restricting. A team offers different perspectives and ideas, which can bring much better results. Studies have shown that teams with members from diverse backgrounds - gender, age, ethnicity and more - are more creative and perform better by up to 35 percent compared to non-diverse teams. Instead of viewing a single side of things, teamwork offers a three-dimensional picture.

3. Teamwork increases productivity. In a team, the workload is shared among members with different knowledge and skills. Members coordinate efforts to do a better job in a shorter time than a single person could. Different people have different problem-solving methods; they generate new ideas and solutions that would be hard for an individual to handle. Effective brainstorming sessions help teams search for innovative ideas and build solutions on each other's ideas.

4. Teamwork provides opportunities for learning. People with different skills, experience levels and abilities working together not only work better and faster. While chatting about work issues they exchange knowledge, grow together and improve their abilities.

5. Teamwork shapes the company's culture. A team that works well together raises a spirit of friendship, loyalty and cooperation that shapes the company's culture. Working in a positive environment increases morale, happiness and satisfaction, creating a feeling of belonging to something bigger. Eventually the team becomes a community in which everyone understands their role. By supporting each other, members build relationships based on trust and mutual respect; positive team relationships make employees more reliable, effective and productive, and these qualities contribute to the success of the company.

g9-economics-ue8-t6.overview: Every business needs money, and getting it requires a plan. This lesson covers the three budgetary requirements of an enterprise - permanent capital, working capital and asset finance - and the financing options from personal savings to venture capital.
objectives: Identify the financial requirements for entrepreneurial ventures
Distinguish permanent capital, working capital and asset finance
Explain why obtaining finance is difficult for entrepreneurial projects
List and order the sources of finance from personal savings to venture capital
Explain how financing manages assets wisely to use capital efficiently
g9-economics-ue8-t6.simple: All businesses need money. Permanent capital finances start-up costs and major expansions and is rewarded by dividends or capital gains. Working capital is short-term financing for raw materials and other running costs. Asset finance is a medium- to long-term loan of 3 to 10 years or more for physical assets such as plants, machinery and vehicles. Entrepreneurial projects find finance hard because they are riskier than established firms. The financing options come in a rough order: personal savings (at least half of start-up funds), friends and relatives, partners, angels (wealthy private investors) and venture capital firms expecting high returns and growth.
g9-economics-ue8-t6.detailed:
Why finance matters. Finding sources of finance is important for many reasons. The development of new products can be costly, and capital may be required. Such developments are financed internally, whereas capital to purchase machinery may come from external sources. Many organisations look for short-term capital in the form of loans and working capital. Financing is more than just getting money; it is a process of managing assets wisely in order to use capital efficiently. The critical issue is to guarantee sufficient cash flow for operations and to plan financing that matches changes in the enterprise.

1. Permanent capital. The permanent capital base of a small firm usually comes from an investment in a share company, personal loans to form partners, or investment in a sole proprietorship. It finances the start-up costs of an enterprise or major developments and expansions in its life cycle, and may be required for significant innovation such as new product development. Ideally, permanent capital is only repaid when the firm can afford it; investment in equity is rewarded by dividends from profits, or a capital gain when shares are sold.

2. Working capital. Working capital is a type of short-term financing. Most small firms need it to pay for raw materials and cover other costs, and requirements vary considerably by business type. In some cases it is sufficient to finance the start-up of a small business, so that suppliers are effectively financing the business. Although normally used to fund trading, it can also purchase short-lived assets such as company vehicles, which may be changed every 4 or 5 years.

3. Asset finance. Asset finance is a medium- to long-term loan. The purchase of physical assets is typically financed over 3 to 10 years or more, depending on the asset's useful life. Plants, machinery, equipment, company vehicles and buildings can all be financed with short-term or long-term loans from a variety of sources.

Why start-ups struggle. Financial requirements change as an enterprise grows, and obtaining resources in the amount needed and at the right time is difficult for entrepreneurial projects because they are generally considered more risky than established enterprises.

Financing options in order. First, entrepreneurs should pay start-up money from personal savings: as a general rule, they should provide at least half of the start-up funds this way. Second, after finishing their own savings, they should turn to friends and relatives willing to invest; the entrepreneur is expected to describe the opportunities and risks of the business. Third, an entrepreneur can take on partners to expand the capital formation of the proposed business. Fourth, angels are wealthy private investors, often entrepreneurs themselves, who invest in start-up businesses in exchange for taking risks. Fifth, venture capital firms are private organisations that invest in new businesses expecting a high return and high growth potential; they provide start-up capital, development funds or expansion funds.

keyTerms.def: The long-term capital base used for start-up costs, major developments and expansions; equity investment rewarded by dividends or capital gains.
Short-term financing needed to pay for raw materials and cover other running costs.
A medium- to long-term loan, typically 3 to 10 years, used to purchase physical assets such as plants, machinery and buildings.
An entrepreneur's own money used to start the business; at least half of start-up funds by the general rule.
Wealthy private investors, often entrepreneurs, who invest in start-up businesses in exchange for taking risks.
A private organisation that invests in new businesses expecting high return and high growth potential, providing start-up, development or expansion funds.
The movement of money in and out of a business, which financing must guarantee to keep operations running.
A share of profits paid to an equity investor in reward for investment.

workedExamples.problem: A start-up needs 100,000 birr to open. Following the general rule, how much should come from personal savings and what order of options follows?
workedExamples.given: Total start-up funds required: 100,000 birr.
workedExamples.formula: Rule: entrepreneurs should provide at least half of the start-up funds from personal savings.
workedExamples.substitution: Half of 100,000 birr is 50,000 birr.
workedExamples.calculation: The remaining 50,000 birr comes from friends and relatives, then partners, then angels, then venture capital firms if needed.
workedExamples.answer: At least 50,000 birr from personal savings; the rest from friends and relatives and later investors in order.

workedExamples.problem: A furniture maker needs (a) monthly cash for paint and nails, (b) money to build a workshop with a 15-year life, and (c) funds for a major expansion of the product line. Match each need to its budgetary requirement.
workedExamples.given: Three needs of different duration and purpose.
workedExamples.formula: Match: running costs = working capital; long-lived assets = asset finance; start-up or major development = permanent capital.
workedExamples.substitution: Paint and nails are raw materials; the workshop is a physical asset; the expansion is a major development.
workedExamples.calculation: Duration and purpose classify each need into the correct category.
workedExamples.answer: (a) working capital, (b) asset finance, (c) permanent capital.

workedExamples.problem: A wealthy retired businessperson invests her own money in a neighbour's new juice processing start-up, accepting the risk. What is she called, and how does she differ from a venture capital firm?
workedExamples.given: An individual investor takes personal risk in a start-up.
workedExamples.formula: Definition check: angels are wealthy individuals; venture capital firms are private organisations expecting high return.
workedExamples.substitution: She is one person, not an organisation, investing mainly as a risk-taker.
workedExamples.calculation: The individual fits the angel definition, not the venture capital definition.
workedExamples.answer: She is an angel; a venture capital firm is an organisation investing for high return and growth.

workedExamples.problem: A supplier delivers raw materials today for a small shop with almost no cash, expecting payment after the goods are sold. Explain how this helps finance the business.
workedExamples.given: The shop pays suppliers after selling their goods.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: working capital can finance start-up so that suppliers effectively finance the business.
workedExamples.substitution: The goods arrived before cash left the shop; inventory is sold first, then the supplier is paid.
workedExamples.calculation: The credit period provides short-term financing without a bank.
workedExamples.answer: Suppliers are effectively financing the business through trade credit covered by working capital.

commonMistakes: Using working capital (short-term) to buy long-lived buildings, when asset finance or permanent capital is appropriate.
Borrowing from investors before exhausting personal savings, against the general rule of providing at least half yourself.
Thinking financing is only about getting money, when it is managing assets wisely to use capital efficiently.
Expecting venture capital firms to fund stable, low-growth businesses; they expect high return and high growth potential.
Forgetting to describe the opportunities and risks of the business when asking friends and relatives to invest.
Ignoring cash flow, the critical issue in financing for operations.
Assuming banks are the only source of finance, ignoring partners, angels and venture capital firms.
applications: Saving part of weekly pocket money or small earnings as personal savings before starting a business project.
Matching each school enterprise need to the right fund type: raw materials, tools, or expansion.
Preparing an honest description of opportunities and risks to present to family members considering investment.
Using supplier credit for raw materials so scarce cash is reserved for daily operations.
Understanding why Ethiopian start-ups are considered riskier than established firms, and planning financing to match growth stages.
Tracking monthly cash flow of a small school kiosk to guarantee enough money for operations.
g9-economics-ue8-t6.summary: An enterprise needs three budgetary categories: permanent capital for start-up and major expansion, working capital for short-term costs like raw materials, and asset finance as a 3 to 10 year loan for physical assets. Entrepreneurial projects find finance difficult because they are riskier than established firms. The recommended order of sources is personal savings of at least half, then friends and relatives, partners, angels, and venture capital firms.

questions.answer: dividends from profits and capital gain when shares are sold|dividends and capital gains
questions.explanation: Equity is rewarded by dividends from profits or a capital gain when shares are sold.

questions.q: Arrange the financing options in the recommended order.
questions.explanation: Personal savings, then friends and relatives, then partners, then angels, then venture capital firms.

questions.q: What is the critical issue in financing that operations require?
questions.explanation: The critical issue in financing is to guarantee sufficient cash flow for operations.
